name: Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN)
analogy: Think of it as a forger and an inspector who are both handed the same order slip, for example 'a quiet London-open morning'. The forger draws a price path to fit the slip, and the inspector checks both whether it looks real and whether it fits the slip.

steps.title: Write the order slip
steps.description: The condition is whatever you want to control: a class label, a regime, a time of day, or even another picture. It is turned into numbers so both networks can read it.
steps.inExample: The slip says: regime high-volatility downtrend, start time 09:35, average true range 31 points.

steps.title: Give the forger noise plus the slip
steps.description: The generator receives a list of random numbers and the slip joined together. The random numbers supply variety and the slip supplies direction, so one slip can produce many different results.
steps.inExample: A list of 32 random numbers is joined to the slip and passed into the generator.

steps.title: Forge a sample that fits the slip
steps.description: The generator produces a sample in the same format as the real data, such as a short run of bar returns, aiming to look like real data that came under that condition.
steps.inExample: The generator outputs 6 five-minute bar returns that mostly fall one after another, with big bodies.

steps.title: Show the inspector real and forged pairs
steps.description: The discriminator sees pairs: a sample together with its slip. Real pairs come from history, forged pairs from the generator. It must catch both a forged sample and a real sample paired with the wrong slip.
steps.inExample: It sees the forged 6-bar run labelled high-volatility downtrend next to real runs with that label and scores each.

steps.title: Both networks improve through the contest
steps.description: When the inspector catches a forgery, the forger learns what gave it away. When the inspector is fooled, the inspector learns. Over many rounds, forgeries for each slip come to resemble real data under that slip.
steps.inExample: After many rounds, forged runs for the downtrend slip have the right size and sequence of moves, and the inspector's scores sit near 50 percent.

steps.title: Generate on demand for any slip
steps.description: Once trained, you choose a slip, draw fresh random numbers, and get a new sample each time. Changing only the slip changes the kind of sample while keeping everything else the same.
steps.inExample: Drawing 3 times with the same slip yields 3 different 6-bar paths: two end 49 and 28 points lower, and one ends 11 points higher after a bounce inside the downtrend.

useFor.example: Generating many plausible 6-bar paths for MNQ 5-minute bars given a high-volatility regime, to stress-test a stop placement rule.

useFor.task: Balancing rare conditions in training data
useFor.example: Creating extra examples of the rare news-spike morning so a direction model does not see only calm days.
Asking for paths at 09:35 versus 15:45 to see how a strategy's results would change with the opening-hour range.
Holding a regime fixed and drawing hundreds of paths to look at the spread of worst-case 30-minute moves.

avoidWhen: You need a trustworthy price forecast rather than plausible examples; a model trained directly on the target, such as gradient boosting, gives a calibrated probability.
You have too little data per condition; a conditional model needs enough real examples of each slip, or the forged samples will simply copy a few real ones.

example.scenario: A researcher wants to see what a high-volatility downtrend looks like over the next 30 minutes on MNQ 5-minute bars, to test whether a 40-point stop survives. They give the trained cGAN the regime and time of day and ask for three paths.

input.summary: The order slip and the number of samples requested.

fields.name: regime label
fields.meaning: The condition the generated paths must fit.

fields.name: start time
fields.meaning: The time of day of the first generated bar.

fields.name: starting price
fields.meaning: The price every generated path starts from.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, used to scale the moves.

fields.name: paths requested
fields.meaning: How many different samples to draw for the same order.

fields.name: bars per path
fields.meaning: Each path covers 6 bars of 5 minutes, which is 30 minutes.

output.summary: Three synthetic 6-bar paths for the same order, each ending at a different price.

fields.name: path A final close
fields.meaning: Where the first generated path ends after 30 minutes, 49 points below the start.

fields.name: path B final close
fields.meaning: Where the second path ends, 28 points below the start.

fields.name: path C final close
fields.meaning: Where the third path ends, 11 points above the start, a bounce inside the downtrend.

fields.name: inspector realness score, average
fields.meaning: How real the inspector finds the three paths on average; near 50 percent means it cannot tell them from history.

example.reading: Paths are examples of what could happen under the slip, not predictions. Run many, look at how far each path falls from the start against the 40-point stop, and compare with how real paths from that regime behaved. If real history and the generated paths disagree, trust history.
